topic: Law fact / myth-buster: a basic 'Act Only' (third-party) motor policy does not automatically cover a free (gratuitous) passenger in a private vehicle - Section 147, MV Act read with Sections 145-149; Section 147(1)(b)(ii) covers passengers of public service vehicles separately; occupant may still be a third party against another negligent vehicle; comprehensive/package policy may cover occupants as per its terms; Article 142 is the Supreme Court's power alone - Tribunals and HCs cannot order pay-and-recover where no liability exists; four-part test for exceptional pay-and-recover; here, insurer told to pay the outstanding Rs 7,79,800 award (MACT Latur, 28 Aug 2017, 7.5% interest) to the widow and sons of a jeep passenger killed in 2012 and recover from the owner (Sukumarbai & Ors. v. United India Insurance Company Ltd. & Anr., 2026 INSC 1272, 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 1212, Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh, 25 Nov 2026)

slides.title: Car insured? Your **passengers** may not be
slides.subtitle: A basic **"Act Only"** policy does not automatically cover a person riding free in a **private vehicle**, says the Supreme Court.
slides.cite: **Sukumarbai & Ors. v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr.** · 2026 INSC 1272 · Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh · 25 Nov 2026

slides.label: The myth
slides.title: "My vehicle is insured, so **everyone** is covered"
bullets: **Fact:** the compulsory cover under **Section 147** of the Motor Vehicles Act does not, by itself, include free riders in a private car or jeep.
The law **separately** covers passengers of public service vehicles like buses and taxis. That shows not every occupant is meant to be covered.
The same rule was applied earlier to **pillion riders** on two-wheelers.

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: A jeep overturned after a **wedding**
bullets: In **2012**, a jeep driven by its owner hit a bridge railing and overturned. A passenger died.
His wife and two sons got **Rs 7,79,800** with 7.5% interest from the Tribunal at Latur, which told the insurer to pay first and recover from the owner.
The **Bombay High Court** removed that direction, as the policy did not cover the passenger.

slides.label: The ruling
slides.title: No cover, but family **not left empty-handed**
bullets: The Supreme Court agreed the insurer had **no legal liability** under the Act Only policy.
Only the Supreme Court can use **Article 142** to make such an insurer pay. Tribunals and High Courts cannot.
Finding the case exceptional, it told the insurer to pay the unpaid award and **recover it from the owner**.
slides.note: **Law fact:** a passenger in your car may still claim as a third party against **another vehicle** whose negligence caused the accident.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: Read your policy **before** you need it
bullets: A **comprehensive or package** policy may cover occupants of a private vehicle, depending on its terms.
The Court warned this exceptional relief must **not** become a substitute for insurance. Owners can end up paying.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Your car is insured. But is the friend in the passenger seat? 🚗⚠️

Myth: "My vehicle is insured, so anyone riding in it is covered." The Supreme Court has said this is not automatically true. A basic "Act Only" (third-party) policy under Section 147 of the Motor Vehicles Act does not, by itself, cover a person riding free in a private vehicle. The law covers passengers of buses and taxis separately, which shows not every occupant is included. A comprehensive or package policy may cover occupants, depending on its terms.

The case: in 2012, a jeep driven by its owner overturned and a passenger died. The Tribunal at Latur awarded his wife and two sons Rs 7,79,800 with interest and asked the insurer to pay first and recover from the owner. The Bombay High Court removed that direction. The Supreme Court agreed the insurer was not liable under the policy, and said only it can use Article 142 to order such payment. Treating the case as exceptional, it asked the insurer to pay the unpaid award and recover it from the owner.

What to do: check what your motor policy actually covers, ask your insurer about cover for occupants, and remember that without it, the owner may have to pay.

Case: Sukumarbai & Ors. v. United India Insurance Company Ltd. & Anr., 2026 INSC 1272
Bench: Justices Vikram Nath, Sandeep Mehta and Aparesh Kumar Singh, Supreme Court (25 Nov 2026)
